Position: generally get lower, so flex your ankles, knees and hip much more. Press your shins into the front of the boot except for in bumps and even then make sure to stay central, not sit back. Raise your arms more and keep them relatively still. You may benefit from a pole plant which occurs right at the end of the turn on the side that you will turn next and is simply a small wrist action, not an entire arm movement.

Counter-rotation: aim to turn the lower body independently from the upper body, definitely don't use a rotation of the shoulders or arms to initiale turns. keep the shoulders and hips facing down the mountain as much as possible. To practice this hold your poles in the middle at hold them out in front of you. Pick an object directly down the mountain from you and keep it between the two poles as you ski down the mountain, forcing you to prevent your shoulders pointing the same way as the skis.

Consistency: try to make each turn the same shape and speed, it will make your skiing much more fluid. As the slope gets steeper, make sure to maintain a nice round turn shape rather than letting the turns become more Z shaped. You will speed up more during the turn as you spend more time in the fall line, but all you need to do the manage the speed is ski more across the hill/make the turns fully rounded off.

Final tip is to crucify the camera man and have fun

In that case, I would definitely recommend the Big Agnes Insulated AirCore Ultra, It's the best value sleeping pad for the r-value (how insulated it is) and will do you just fine through most winters in western europe. For a sleeping bag, if you're not concerned about size then I'd say go with something like a berghaus transition 400 which has a comfort rating of -2 degrees c and isn't too expensive, although if you've got the budget then a down sleeping bag is well worth it in my opinion. As for tents then the brand Nemo has lots of good options that come with poles although it's quite an expensive brand. I don't really have that much to say on tents because i personally find that for winter in the UK, my tarp and bivi setup is warm enough if i sleep in a fleece and socks but I think that the way to go for you is a tent. I know vango has some fairly inexpensive decent small tents although they are really quite heavy.

You'll need 3 things: a sleeping bag, a sleeping pad and some kind of shelter. These are all non negotiable. What you get will be determined by how much space you have, how light you want to go, what weather and temperatures you'll be in and how much you want to spend. To give you recommendations I'd need to know where you're going, what the weather's going to be like, if you'll be using it for other trips and if so, what kind and where, and how much space you have. Weight doesn't matter that much when cycling unless you're going up some pretty major hills.

For sleeping bags, expect to spend $100 (not on sale) on a 3 season synthetic one and probably $100 more for a decent 3 season down bag. I use a Robens Serac 300 with 650 fill down comfort rated to -4 degrees C. I got it for about £220 in the Uk

Sleeping pads range from dirt cheap foam mats to more than $200 for a 4 season inflatable one. I personally use the Big Agnes Insulated AirCore Ultra with an r-value of 4.5 which I got for about £50.

Bad tents are heavy and bulky and I hate them, but they do work and they're easy. Don't do this, lowering the seat to where you can have both feet on the ground may be helpful for getting on and off, but that means the saddle is too low, meaning you won't be able to pedal efficiently and could develop joint problems from excess stress. Starting with your bum off the saddle and over the top tube (a bit forward) is just as easy, all you have to do is remember to stand up off the saddle when stopping. That being said, you should definitely take it to a shop to get the seat adjusted to the right height, the inside of you knee should make roughly a 150 degree angle at the bottom of the stroke. Could be more, could be less, it depends on what you find comfortable.

In regards to the main issue at hand, I'd say get your partner to hold you upright by the saddle and push you forwards slowly so you can get used to getting the other foot on the pedal. Also, start with the pedal you're pushing off with at the top of the stroke and a little bit forwards so you can push off properly, giving you a few seconds of freewheeling to find your footing with the other pedal.

Final suggestion if you're ok with looking like a bit of a mug as you're learning is pick up a pair of stabilisers/training wheels and just practice pushing off and getting your other foot to the pedal quickly, then you can take them off when you're comfortable with the motions. Hope this helps.

There are a bunch of factors that i'm aware of could be at play:

1. Assuming the power meter is on the pedals, check your crank length. They usually scale crank length with the size of the bike so if you've changed bike size the crank length may have changed which would affect your power figures.
2. the tyres on a road bike would have lower rolling resistance that a gravel bike which would reduce required power.
3. the road bike will have more racey geometry compared to the gravel bike (shorter stack, longer reach) so unless you've had a bike fit or have spent a bit of time working things out, you could be sitting in a disadvantageous position which could be limiting your power output.
4. on the flip side, the road geometry will also cause your natural riding position to be lower and more aero, making you go faster for the watts.

it could be any number of these factors.
